sentences.text: The recording is about to begin.
Turn to page 3 of the data file.
Hi listeners. Welcome to Nosing Around, Hong Kong’s leading weekly podcast for teenagers.
teenagers. On a packed program this week, we have: A report on what it’s like to be a die hard fan of local Hong Kong football, as we invite in in May.
of the supporters clubs of the ten teams in the Hong Kong Premier League.
We have An interview with Dr.
Have, a Singaporean hotel director who combines his day job with being a DJ at nights.
But firstly, I’ll be interviewing a very different doctor.
I have with me today Dr.
Jack Jones from the Hong Kong Social History Museum.
Dr. Jones, welcome back to Nozing Around.
This is the third time I think you’ve been on the show.
Hello Patty. Yes, it’s great to be back on Nozing Around.
It’s always a pleasure.
So, maybe we can start with the Social History Museum.
I’m sure our listeners will be familiar with what is meant by a museum traditionally, but can you explain to our listeners what what a social history museum is?
Well, Patti, that’s a good question.
A social history museum is a place where visitors can experience what daily life was like for ordinary people in the past.
OK. So everyday life for ordinary people in the past.
When you say ordinary people, do you mean people like me and the listeners not say kings and queens?
Yes, ordinary people like you and me, not kings and queens.
You are not a queen, I’m guessing.
Well, maybe in a past life.
So what sort of things can I see in a social history museum?
Well, You see ordinary items people used in the past.
So rather than seeing ancient pottery and weapons, we can look at old tables and chairs you would find in your grandparents homes things like old telephones, computers So ordinary things then.
But old. Would that include old clothes people used to wear?
Yes, exactly. You see, that would interest me.
I really like vintage fashion items jackets, jewellery, that sort of thing.
Now, I’ve heard your museum is very big.
In fact, fact, it’s so big that you’ve even rebuilt a whole farmhouse inside the museum building.
Yes, that’s right the Wang Chung traditional farmhouse.
It was moved to the museum brick by brick and reconstructed inside the museum last year in 2015.
It was a very difficult operation, I can tell you.
And where did it originally come from?
The farmhouse was was found at the bottom of a reservoir, you know, a man -made lake.
Wow! You mean the farmhouse was under water?
Yes, at the bottom of the Wangchung Reservoir.
OK, I know Wangchung Reservoir.
I’ve been hiking up there.
Well, maybe what you didn’t know was before the reservoir, there was a village there Wangchung Village.
Village. And it disappeared underwater in 1990 when they built the reservoir.
Really? No, I didn’t know that.
It actually used to be quite a famous village Wang Chun, for the Wang Chun Pineapple Festival.
OK, the pineapple festival.
I think I might have seen old photos of that.
Yes, quite possibly.
The Pineapple Festival was a pretty big festival in its day.
Farmers Farmers would offer pineapples to the god of farming.
Yeah, that's what I remember from the photo.
Right Oh, I know what I was going to ask you’ll have to forgive me, but where is the Social History Museum?
It’s in South Point, close to the new MTR station.
Well, that’s convenient.
Yeah, only two minutes from South Point MTR, Exit A.
Wow. Only two minutes walk.
Is that on Reed Street?
You know, as in R -E -I -D?
Yes, that’s right.
Get out at Exit A and just go straight up Reed Street to the museum.
And I’ve been told that you are giving a talk on Farming in The New Territories.
Is that next Wednesday, the 13th of April?
Yes, that’s right on April 13th from 8 to 9 in the evening, evening, Wednesday.
The title of the talk, as you just said, is Farming in The New Territories.
OK, that sounds very interesting.
I’d love to know more about farming in the New Territories, wouldn’t you listeners?
Remember, if you want to go, don’t be late 8pm start and finish at 9pm.
Can I also add that we’re having an exhibition on Farming in The New Territories at the the museum.
And in the exhibition we’re hoping to display the Chang 'e Tak plow.
Oh, I actually remember reading about the Chang 'e Tak plow when I studied history at school.
A lot of our listeners will remember it from school as well, I’m sure.
Actually, I’d be really interested in seeing it.
Maybe you could tell the listeners who don’t know what’s so special about the Chang 'e Tak plow.
Well, it’s special because it’s the only wood and iron plow in the world that So hang on, hang on, there are no other wood and iron plows in the world?
No Patty, I hadn’t quite finished what I was saying.
I was about to say that there are of course many wood and iron plows in the world, but this is the only one from the 18th Century that’s not damaged.
So that’s the amazing thing about the Chang 'e tack plow.
it’s from the 18th Century but is in almost perfect condition.
OK, well as I said, I want to go to see it for real.
OK, thank you for coming in and speaking with us today, Dr.
Jones, and good luck with your ex -sevition.
